title: Alone, not lonely
hook: being alone isn't loneliness; learn to be at ease by yourself (Discourses 3.13)
carry: someone you can live with is there

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was askēsis, training kept private: spit out the cold water and tell no one. Your line was privately.

A party of two hundred people can be lonelier than a quiet walk by yourself. Some people who live alone are deeply at ease, while some who are never alone feel stranded. A full calendar doesn't promise company, and an empty room doesn't promise loneliness. Epictetus heard people in crowded Rome say they'd been left all alone.
screen: `LONELY AT A PARTY OF TWO HUNDRED.` → `AT EASE ON A QUIET WALK.` → `FORLORN IN A GREAT CITY.`

segments.voice: Discourses book three, chapter thirteen: what solitude is. Epictetus separates two things we usually blur. Being alone doesn't make someone forlorn, any more than a crowd makes them not forlorn. When we lose a brother, a child or a friend, we say we've been left all alone, even while living in Rome, with crowds in the street and neighbors on every side. So what is the forlorn feeling, really? Being without help, he says: exposed, at the mercy of whatever comes. Then an image from Stoic belief about the cosmos. In the Stoic picture he's drawing on, the world goes through cycles, and at the end of each it's drawn back into fire. In that moment, Zeus is alone. Yet he isn't forlorn. He's at rest with himself, thinking about how things are ordered. We should be able to do something like that: talk with ourselves, be at peace without needing others, not be lost when there's no one to fill the hours. Then a contrast. The emperor gives the world a great peace: no wars, no pirates, safe roads. But he can't give peace from fever, shipwreck, grief or envy. That inner peace has to be learned. One of its first lessons is sitting in an empty room and finding that someone you can live with is there.
screen: `ALONE ISN'T THE SAME AS FORLORN.` · `FORLORN MEANS WITHOUT HELP.` · `ZEUS ALONE, AT REST WITH HIMSELF.` · `A PEACE NO EMPEROR CAN GIVE.` · then, large: `ALONE, NOT LONELY.`

segments.voice: Sit somewhere you can be by yourself, even a corner, and notice whether being alone feels restful, a little uneasy, or both. Without reaching for your phone, ask yourself gently, the way a friend would: how are you, really? Listen, and let the quiet be enough for a while.
Alone. Epictetus on solitude: being by yourself isn't the same as being forlorn, and we can learn to be at ease in our own company.
Your line: someone you can live with is there. Being by yourself and being forlorn are two different things. That's day four hundred twenty-one.

howItsDone: Some people drawn to Stoicism set aside a short time each day to be alone without distractions, treating it as practice in being at ease with themselves.

notes: Discourses 3.13 paraphrased: solitude as the condition of a helpless person; being alone vs. being forlorn; losing a brother/son/friend while in Rome amid crowds; Zeus at the conflagration, alone and at rest; conversing with oneself; Caesar's peace (no wars, robbers, pirates) vs. peace from fever, shipwreck, grief, envy. Confirm.
Reviewer edit: Rome softened to 'one of the biggest cities in the world' (whether it was the largest, vs. e.g. Han Luoyang, is debated); screen line changed to 'forlorn in a great city'.
Reviewer edit: 'The Stoics taught' cyclical conflagration softened to 'Many Stoics taught'; some Stoics (e.g. Panaetius, Boethus) doubted ekpyrōsis.
Loneliness can be painful and serious; the script frames being at ease alone as a practice, not as a dismissal of loneliness. Check tone.
